title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). Using a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 per topology class) we produced one shared initial candidate per task with gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and evaluated the same candidate under both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforced structured workflow policies and could trigger one repair iteration per guarded episode. Observed outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces show repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We (1) present the preregistered confirmatory result and execution accounting, (2) add a compact, formal scoring definition and a concrete scoring example drawn from archived artifacts, (3) provide a nearest-work comparison matrix contrasting our shared-generation paired design with closest prior studies, and (4) discuss design trade-offs and concrete follow-up recommendations for experiments intended to exercise repair behavior.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) can translate operator intent into device-level configuration commands, yet syntactically plausible outputs can violate workflow invariants (for example, changing MTU without a required shutdown or performing unsafe uplink switchover). Such semantic failures are often visible only when commands are executed in stateful emulators or production devices. Prior work therefore recommends integrating verification, emulation, or veto layers; empirical benchmarks that run closed-loop emulation have revealed sequencing and stateful errors that token-level checks miss. However, most prior experimental designs conflate generator variance with validator efficacy (generator-focused evaluations), making it difficult to isolate the marginal utility of a validator and a bounded repair policy.

We address a narrowly scoped confirmatory question using a shared-generation paired design: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow, when the generator output is held fixed? The preregistered paired design produces one shared initial candidate per task and scores that candidate both as baseline (LLM-only) and as guarded (validator±repair). Holding generator output fixed removes generator-induced variance and isolates the validator/repair marginal effect. The risk is that, if the generator rarely produces invalid candidates under the chosen prompt and task bank, the guarded arm will not exercise repairs and the confirmatory test will be uninformative; we preregistered this trade-off and planned sensitivity analyses.
sections.related_work:
Executable-benchmark and NetOps verification work demonstrate that closed-loop emulation exposes operational failure modes beyond syntax: make-before-break mistakes, group-availability violations, and ordered-field constraints. Representative recent artifacts (verified) include NetConfArena (an executable closed-loop benchmark) and several 2026 benchmark/repair studies that evaluate closed-loop behavior. A parallel literature investigates tool-augmented agent architectures and bounded-autonomy guardrails (veto layers, canaries, translation-to-formal-model, and generate→validate→repair pipelines) as operational safety measures. Those works motivate the guarded pipeline tested here but generally evaluate end-to-end generator-plus-validator systems where generator variability and validator effects are not isolated.

This compact matrix emphasizes that closed-loop emulation appears repeatedly in the literature; by contrast, the explicit shared-generation paired design used here (one identical generator output scored under both conditions) is the methodological novelty we employ to measure validator/repair marginal effects independent of generator sampling variability.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan. The experiment was preregistered (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) before execution. Preregistered design: paired-binary confirmatory test (exact two-sided McNemar) on paired pass/fail labels across N=120 tasks partitioned into three topology classes (40 per class). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Analysis used an exact McNemar test and a bootstrap-percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729). The preregistration specified deterministic reset controls, contamination checks, a repair budget (≤1 repair per guarded episode), exclusion rules for instrumentation failures, and sensitivity analyses treating technical exclusions as failures.

Task generation, harness, and execution summary. Tasks were deterministically produced (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). Each task manifest includes initial_state, expected_final_state, natural-language intent, required_sequence (canonical ordered operations), and difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, difficulty level). The declared generator was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json recorded); the run used a single shared-initial_generation stage with model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair) to isolate validator effects. The guarded pipeline invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0) which runs candidates in an emulator and enforces structured workflow policies (for example: must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, make-before-break). The validator can trigger at most one repair iteration per guarded episode (repair policy prespecified).

Compact provenance paragraph (condensed artifact pointers). To keep the main narrative focused we condense archival provenance to a compact pointer paragraph. All primary execution and analysis artifacts required to reproduce the reported accounting are archived and checksummed. Representative artifact names (archived in the manuscript bundle) include: execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, execution/responses/*, execution/scoring/task-0000XX-*.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json, and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. The preregistration manifest and immutable initial master prompt are archived and referenced in the disclosure. (Full artifact listings and checksums reside in the archived execution manifest and are not reproduced inline.)

Formal binary scoring rule (compact, artifact-grounded). The preregistered pass/fail label used by the McNemar test is a deterministic mapping from archived scoring/scorer/validator fields to a binary outcome per episode:
Decision rule (applied to each scored episode):
- PASS iff (scorer.score == 1) AND (validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true).
- FAIL otherwise.
Notes: scorer.score is the documented per-episode integer (scoring_rule = "full_intent_constraint_validation"). validator_trace.validation_after.valid is the emulator/validator boolean indicating whether the candidate satisfied task-encoded workflow constraints. Both fields are present in archived scoring JSON artifacts.

Concrete example (artifact-grounded): execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json records scorer.score = 1, scoring_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION", and validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true; normalized_response equals normalized_reference_answer. Under the decision rule above that episode is labeled PASS. Conversely, an episode with validator_trace.validation_after.valid = false (or scorer.score != 1) would be labeled FAIL. The analysis pipeline applied this rule to derive the 120 paired binary labels per condition used in the confirmatory McNemar test.
sections.results:
Execution and primary confirmatory outcome. The run completed without technical exclusions: planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). analysis/condition_summary.csv records baseline successes = 120, baseline failures = 0, guarded successes = 120, guarded failures = 0 (success rates = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) shows n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p-value = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00. Bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Validator traces report repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes and validator.violation_count = 0 in analysis artifacts; consequently no repair artifacts were generated.

Per-topology counts (preregistered deterministic partition). The task manifest deterministically assigned 40 tasks per topology class. Per-topology outcomes (from representative scoring artifacts and analysis summaries) are: Edge: baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40; Core: baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40; Leaf–spine: baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40. These per-topology counts appear in the archived scoring JSON and analysis/condition_summary.csv; a compact table is reported in the manuscript captions.

Diagnostics and reconciliation. analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120 and zero technical/instrumentation exclusions. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty. deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms provider-call audits and pair accounting (hosted_model_call_event_count = 120; cache_miss_count = 120; cross-condition cache reuse = false). Representative scoring artifacts (for example execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json) show parsed_command_count equals required_command_count and validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true, supporting the scoring-rule mapping used in the confirmatory analysis.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: ceiling outcome and what it implies. The shared-generation paired design isolates validator/repair marginal effects by holding generator output fixed. In this run the generator produced valid candidates for every selected task under the frozen prompt and declared model; the validator therefore never applied repairs. The observed exact McNemar p = 1.0 and degenerate bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00] are direct statistical consequences of n_10 = n_01 = 0 (no discordant pairs). This outcome does not imply that validators or repairs are unnecessary in general; rather, it documents that for the chosen generator/prompt/task-bank combination repair utility was not exercised.

Design lessons and concrete recommendations (artifact-grounded). Based on archived task difficulty metadata (dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, difficulty level) and the absence of repair activity, we recommend future confirmatory designs intended to evaluate repair utility include one or more of: (1) independent per-condition generation (allow separate generator samples per condition) or stratified paired designs that pair tasks by block but permit condition-specific generation; (2) controlled prompt perturbations targeted to task manifest entries labeled 'very_hard' or with high dependency_rule_count; (3) prespecified task selection concentrating power on tasks where generator errors are plausibly frequent; (4) expanded exploratory repair budgets permitting multiple repair iterations to observe repair convergence behavior. These recommendations are implementable using the archived task_manifest difficulty fields without changing harness semantics.

Threats to validity (concise). Internal validity: strong—deterministic provisioning, exhaustive provider-call audit logs, zero exclusions, and reproducible validator traces. Construct validity: limited by the validator policy encodings derived from synthetic task payloads; validator emulation may not capture all vendor- or telemetry-specific behaviors. External validity: constrained by the synthetic deterministic task corpus, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power assumption (baseline ≈0.40) was violated by an observed baseline = 0.00; consequently the confirmatory test is uninformative for the originally targeted absolute reduction.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact-rich paired experiment (N=120) that compared an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow while holding generator outputs fixed. All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, producing concordant success in both conditions (n_11 = 120) and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The principal scientific contribution is methodological: the shared-generation paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair marginal effects and, with deterministic archival artifacts (task manifests, validator traces, provider-call audits, reconciliation files), supports reproducible failure analysis and transparent auditing even when the primary test is degenerate. The archived artifacts enable targeted follow-up experiments (for example, independent per-condition generation, targeted perturbations, or concentrated sampling on 'very_hard' tasks) to better exercise repair utilities under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
